title: Exhaustiveness and absolute simplicity of rational highest-weight Lie modules
statement:
Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra over $\mathbf Q$ [def-wf-lie-algebra, def-wf-semisimple-lie-algebra], and let $\mathfrak h$ be maximal abelian with all adjoint operators diagonalizable over $\mathbf Q$. Use its root spaces, roots $R$, normalized coroot elements $h_\alpha$, and a simple-root base $\Delta=\{\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r\}$ as in [lem-sfb-split-semisimple-root-decomposition]; a base is a basis of $\mathfrak h^\vee$ in which roots have integer coordinates all of one sign. Let $P=\{\lambda\in\mathfrak h^\vee:\lambda(h_\alpha)\in\mathbf Z\text{ for every }\alpha\in R\}$ and $P^+=\{\lambda\in P:\lambda(h_{\alpha_i})\geq0\text{ for every }i\}$. For each $\lambda\in P^+$ choose a simple module $L(\lambda)$ and a cyclic highest vector as supplied by [lem-sfb-rational-highest-weight-modules]. A Lie module is a vector space with a linear action satisfying $[x,y]v=x(yv)-y(xv)$; a highest vector of weight $\lambda$ is nonzero, has $hv=\lambda(h)v$, and is killed by every positive root space. Simple means nonzero with no nonzero proper invariant subspace.

Every finite-dimensional $\mathfrak g$-module over $\mathbf Q$ is a finite direct sum of the $L(\lambda)$. The modules $L(\lambda)$ are pairwise nonisomorphic, every $\mathfrak g$-linear endomorphism of $L(\lambda)$ is a rational scalar, and every simple module containing a highest vector of weight $\lambda$ is isomorphic to $L(\lambda)$. Each $L(\lambda)$ is absolutely simple, meaning its scalar extension to every field extension of $\mathbf Q$ is simple. The highest-weight line in $L(\lambda)$ is one-dimensional, and any vector killed by all positive root spaces is on that line. The ordinary simultaneous $\mathfrak h$-eigenspaces of every finite-dimensional module form a finite direct sum decomposition with weights in $P$. The empty direct sum gives the zero module. When $\mathfrak g=0$, the only simple module is $L(0)=\mathbf Q$.

source.place: Theorem 23.70 proof (a),(b),(d), printed pp.507--508: Weyl complete reducibility and the standard description of semisimple Lie representations; this node states the independent Lie-theoretic input, not the integration conclusion. Split rational highest-weight classification, uniqueness and absolute simplicity: Serre, Complex Semisimple Lie Algebras, Chapter VII (WANTED locally); rational form follows from the highest-weight construction.

proof.text: First prove complete reducibility over $\mathbf Q$. The algebra $\mathfrak g$ is perfect: [lem-sfb-split-semisimple-root-decomposition] says its coroots span $\mathfrak h$, each coroot is a bracket of opposite root vectors, and $[h_\alpha,x]=2x$ for $x\in\mathfrak g_\alpha$. Thus both $\mathfrak h$ and every root space lie in the span of brackets. The same argument covers $\mathfrak g=0$. By [lem-sfb-perfect-lie-hyperplane-criterion] it suffices to split every simple invariant hyperplane $W$ in every finite-dimensional rational module $M$ for this fixed $\mathfrak g$. Fix such $M,W$, and write $r:\mathfrak g\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbf Q}(M)$ for the action.

source.place: Theorem 23.70(a), printed p.507, Weyl input; Lemma 22.40, printed pp.476-477, in its Lie-module form. Perfectness follows directly from the supplied root brackets.

proof.text: If $r=0$, any linear complement of $W$ is invariant. Otherwise let $\mathfrak a=r(\mathfrak g)$, a nonzero finite-dimensional rational Lie algebra with the commutator bracket. The map $r:\mathfrak g\twoheadrightarrow\mathfrak a$ preserves brackets, so [lem-sfb-semisimple-lie-surjective-image] makes $\mathfrak a$ semisimple. Its inclusion in $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbf Q}(M)$ is faithful. Hence [lem-sfb-faithful-semisimple-trace-form] gives a nondegenerate form $B(x,y)=\operatorname{Tr}_M(xy)$ on $\mathfrak a$. Choose a basis $x_1,\ldots,x_d$ and its $B$-dual basis $x^1,\ldots,x^d$, and define the actual endomorphism $c=\sum_i x_i x^i$ of $M$. Here $d=\dim\mathfrak a>0$.

source.place: Section 22c, The Casimir operator, printed p.475: pass to the image of a representation before defining its Casimir; Proposition 22.41, printed p.477.

proof.text:
Trace cyclicity [lem-pc-finite-dimensional-trace-cyclic] gives $B([z,x],y)+B(x,[z,y])=0$ by expanding the brackets. If $[z,x_i]=\sum_j a_{ji}x_j$, pairing with the dual basis gives $[z,x^i]=-\sum_j a_{ij}x^j$. Therefore
$$[z,c]=\sum_{i,j}a_{ji}x_jx^i-\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}x_ix^j=0$$
by interchanging $i,j$. Thus $c$ commutes with the action. The matrix definition [def-weil-endomorphism-trace] also gives $\operatorname{Tr}_M(c)=\sum_i B(x_i,x^i)=d$. These are finite sums over a rational basis; no integration to an algebraic group is used.

source.place: Section 22c, printed p.475: the dual-basis Casimir commutation and trace calculation, written out in matrices.

proof.text: The action on $M/W$ is zero: its endomorphisms are scalars, hence their commutators vanish, and $\mathfrak g$ is perfect by step 1. Consequently every $x\in\mathfrak a$ maps $M$ into $W$, so $c(M)\subseteq W$. In a basis adapted to $W$, the quotient block of $c$ is zero; hence $\operatorname{Tr}_W(c|_W)=d\ne0$. Put $a=c|_W$. This is a nonzero equivariant endomorphism of the simple module $W$, so its invariant kernel is zero. Since $W$ is finite-dimensional, $a$ is invertible. The map $p=a^{-1}c:M\to W$ is equivariant and restricts to $1_W$. Thus $D=\ker p$ is invariant and $M=W\oplus D$, as seen from $m=p(m)+(m-p(m))$. This verifies the antecedent of [lem-sfb-perfect-lie-hyperplane-criterion]. It follows that every invariant subspace of every finite-dimensional rational $\mathfrak g$-module has an invariant complement. Induct on dimension: in a nonzero module choose an invariant subspace of least positive dimension, which is simple, split it off and apply the induction hypothesis to its smaller complement. The zero-dimensional base is the empty sum. This gives a finite direct sum of simple rational modules.

source.place: Lemma 22.40 and Proposition 22.41, printed pp.476-477. The rational-field argument replaces scalar Schur by the invariant kernel and finite-dimensional invertibility of c restricted to W.

proof.text: We next determine the ordinary Cartan weights without assuming them in advance. Fix any rational endomorphisms $E,F,H$ of a finite-dimensional space satisfying $[H,E]=2E$, $[H,F]=-2F$, $[E,F]=H$. By [lem-sfb-sl2-invariant-complement], repeated choice of a least-dimensional nonzero invariant subspace and splitting decomposes this space into simple modules for these three operators. Fix one such simple rational summand $S$. Over $\overline{\mathbf Q}$, the characteristic polynomial of $H$ has a root, giving an eigenvector $u\ne0$. The nonzero vectors $E^ju$ have distinct $H$-eigenvalues $\mu+2j$, by $HE^j=E^jH+2jE^j$, so finite dimension forces a last nonzero one. It is killed by $E$. Regard the three operators as a representation of the trace-zero $2$ by $2$ matrix Lie algebra, with standard $h=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\ne0$. Apply [lem-sfb-sl2-primitive-lowering-string] over $\overline{\mathbf Q}$ to this vector: its $H$-eigenvalue is an integer $n\ge0$. The rational matrix system $(H-n)w=0$, $Ew=0$ therefore has a nonzero solution over $\overline{\mathbf Q}$. Gaussian elimination has the same pivots after a field extension, so it already has a nonzero rational solution $w\in S$.

source.place: Theorem 23.70(d), printed pp.507-508, integral weight grading prerequisite. Explicit rank-one argument by Q80; primitive weight integrality is the existing Mathlib leaf (Sl2.lean, exists_nat).

proof.text: For this rational $w$, [lem-sfb-sl2-primitive-lowering-string] gives $F^iw\ne0$ for $0\le i\le n$ and $EF^{i+1}w=(i+1)(n-i)F^iw$. The bracket $HF-FH=-2F$ gives $HF^iw=(n-2i)F^iw$ by induction. By [lem-sfb-sl2-primitive-string-vanishing], $F^{n+1}w=0$. Thus the span of $w,Fw,\ldots,F^nw$ is nonzero and stable under all three operators. It equals $S$ by simplicity. Its spanning vectors are independent, being eigenvectors with distinct eigenvalues. Consequently $H$ is diagonalizable with integer eigenvalues on $S$, and therefore on the original direct sum. This proves the rank-one conclusion for every rational triple, including the zero action (where each simple summand has $n=0$).

source.place: Theorem 23.70(d), printed pp.507-508, rank-one input; Mathlib/Algebra/Lie/Sl2.lean, primitive lowering formula and terminal vanishing (the two cited leaves).

proof.text: For an arbitrary finite-dimensional $\mathfrak g$-module $V$, choose normalized simple-root triples $e_i,f_i,h_i$ using [lem-sfb-split-semisimple-root-decomposition]. Their actions satisfy step 5's three identities, so step 6 makes each $h_i$ diagonalizable over $\mathbf Q$ with integer eigenvalues. The root pairing from that node and [lem-sfb-root-base-rational-integral-spans] show that the $h_i$ form a rational basis of $\mathfrak h$ and every coroot is an integral combination of them. Since the $h_i$ commute, their eigenspace decompositions refine each other: the spectral projectors of $h_i$ are the polynomials $\prod_{b\ne a}(h_i-b)/(a-b)$ over its distinct eigenvalues, and commute with every $h_j$. Applying these finitely many commuting projectors gives a finite direct sum of common eigenspaces. A nonzero common eigenspace defines the linear weight $\mu$ by its eigenvalues on the basis $h_i$. Since these eigenvalues are integers, evaluating on integral combinations proves $\mu(h_\alpha)\in\mathbf Z$ for every root, that is $\mu\in P$. The basis of $\mathfrak h$ shows these are precisely its ordinary simultaneous eigenspaces.

source.place: Theorem 23.70(d), printed pp.507-508, the P(root system)-gradation. Rational simultaneous spectral projections and integral coroot coordinates are spelled out.

proof.text:
Let $S$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional simple $\mathfrak g$-module. Its finite weight set from step 7 has a maximal element $\lambda$ for the order $\mu\le
u$ meaning $

For $v\in S_\lambda\setminus\{0\}$ and $x\in\mathfrak g_\alpha$, the identity $h(xv)=x(hv)+[h,x]v$ puts $xv$ in weight $\lambda+\alpha$. If $\alpha$ is positive, maximality forces $xv=0$. For each simple triple, $h_i
e0$ since $\alpha_i(h_i)=2$. Thus [lem-sfb-sl2-primitive-lowering-string], now with $A=\mathfrak g$, gives $\lambda(h_i)\in\mathbf Z_{\ge0}$. Together with step 7, $\lambda\in P^+$. The invariant span of all products of elements of $\mathfrak g$ applied to $v$ is nonzero, so equals $S$. The associative algebra $U$ and left ideal $I_\lambda$ in [lem-sfb-verma-monomial-weight-basis] therefore give a surjection $M(\lambda)	o S$, $u+I_\lambda\mapsto uv$: each generator of $I_\lambda$ kills $v$.

source.place: Theorem 23.70(b),(d), printed pp.507-508, standard Lie representation input. Agent expansion of the maximal-weight and explicit Verma quotient argument; Serre, Complex Semisimple Lie Algebras, Chapter VII, WANTED locally.

proof.text: For any $\eta$, the basis of [lem-sfb-verma-monomial-weight-basis] makes $M(\eta)$ a direct sum of weight spaces, with top space $\mathbf Qv_\eta$ and all weights in $\eta-\mathbf Z_{\ge0}\Delta$. Every vector has finite weight support. If $N$ is an invariant proper subspace and $z\in N$, choose $h\in\mathfrak h$ separating the distinct weights in that support together with $\eta$. Such an $h$ exists over $\mathbf Q$: the product of their nonzero pairwise differences is a nonzero polynomial, which cannot vanish at every rational point (induct on the number of variables). Lagrange interpolation in $h$ extracts the $\eta$ component of $z$ and preserves $N$. That component must be zero, or $N$ contains $v_\eta$ and hence all of $M(\eta)$. The sum $J$ of all proper invariant subspaces thus has zero top component and is proper. It contains every proper subspace, so is the unique maximal one. The kernel of every simple quotient is maximal and hence equals $J$. Apply this to step 8's quotient $S$ and the chosen simple cyclic $L(\lambda)$ of [lem-sfb-rational-highest-weight-modules]: both are $M(\lambda)/J$. This also proves that any simple module, even if initially not assumed finite-dimensional, with a highest vector of weight $\lambda$ is isomorphic to $L(\lambda)$, because that vector generates it. The top weight space of $L(\lambda)$ is one-dimensional, being the nonzero image of the top space of $M(\lambda)$; no other weight maps into that space, by the same finite-support projectors.

source.place: Theorem 23.70(b),(d), printed pp.507-508; explicit rational Verma simple-quotient proof supplied by Q80. Serre, Complex Semisimple Lie Algebras, Chapter VII, WANTED locally.

proof.text: Write $Z=\{w\in L(\lambda):\mathfrak n^+w=0\}$. It is preserved by $\mathfrak h$: for a positive root vector $x$, $x(hw)=h(xw)-[h,x]w=0$. Thus the finite spectral projectors from step 7 show $Z$ is a sum of its ordinary weight spaces. If $0\ne w\in Z$ has weight $\mu$, simplicity says it generates $L(\lambda)$. The same left-ideal argument gives a surjection $M(\mu)\to L(\lambda)$. By [lem-sfb-verma-monomial-weight-basis], its target has weights in $\mu-\mathbf Z_{\ge0}\Delta$, so the occurring weight $\lambda$ satisfies $\lambda\le\mu$. On the other hand, [lem-sfb-rational-highest-weight-modules] puts every weight of $L(\lambda)$ below $\lambda$, so $\mu\le\lambda$. Hence $\mu=\lambda$. Step 9's multiplicity-one result now gives $Z=L(\lambda)_\lambda=\mathbf Qv_\lambda$.

source.place: Theorem 23.70(b),(d), printed pp.507-508, highest-weight input. Agent argument via the two opposite Verma cone inequalities, not an assertion about algebraic group invariants.

proof.text: An isomorphism $L(\lambda)\to L(\mu)$ sends the common positive-root kernel onto the corresponding kernel and preserves the $\mathfrak h$-action. By step 10 these are lines of weights $\lambda,\mu$, so $\lambda=\mu$. Conversely the fixed choice is the same module when the weights agree. Every equivariant endomorphism of $L(\lambda)$ preserves its top line and hence sends $v_\lambda$ to $a v_\lambda$ for some $a\in\mathbf Q$. It then agrees with $a$ times the identity on every product $x_1\cdots x_t v_\lambda$, which span the module. Thus its endomorphisms are exactly rational scalars.

source.place: Agent consequences of steps 9-10 and the cyclicity already supplied; scalar a=0 is included.

proof.text: Let $K/\mathbf Q$ be any field extension. Tensor the ordinary weight decomposition of $L=L(\lambda)$ to obtain $L_K=\bigoplus_\mu K\otimes L_\mu$. A rational element of $\mathfrak h$ separating this finite weight set still separates it over $K$, so the same Lagrange projectors show any $\mathfrak g_K$-invariant $K$-subspace is a direct sum of its intersections with these spaces. Choose a finite rational basis $x_1,\ldots,x_N$ of $\mathfrak n^+$ using [lem-sfb-split-semisimple-root-decomposition]. Its common kernel is the kernel of the single rational matrix $L\to L^N$, $w\mapsto(x_jw)_j$. Row reduction over $\mathbf Q$ computes that kernel; its pivots stay nonzero over $K$, so its kernel after extension is $K\otimes Z=Kv_\lambda$ by step 10. If $W\subset L_K$ is a nonzero invariant subspace, choose a maximal weight among its nonzero weight intersections. Any nonzero vector in that intersection is killed by every positive root space, by the root-weight shift calculation in step 8. It lies in $Kv_\lambda$, so $W$ contains $v_\lambda$. The cyclic products from [lem-sfb-rational-highest-weight-modules] still span after tensoring, giving $W=L_K$. Also $L_K\ne0$, since $v_\lambda$ is part of a rational basis and remains nonzero. This proves absolute simplicity for arbitrary, including transcendental, field extensions.

source.place: Theorem 23.70(b),(d), printed pp.507-508, split rational highest-weight input; explicit finite-matrix scalar-extension proof by Q80. No algebraic-closedness or semisimplicity of the extended module is assumed.

proof.text: The finite simple-summand decomposition from step 4 and steps 8-9 express every finite-dimensional module as a finite direct sum of the selected $L(\lambda)$. Steps 7 and 9-12 prove every other asserted clause. For the zero module use the empty sum. If $\mathfrak g=0$, then $\mathfrak h=0$ and $R=\Delta=\varnothing$, so $P=P^+=\{0\}$. Every subspace is invariant; a nonzero simple module must have dimension one. The specified choice [lem-sfb-rational-highest-weight-modules] is $L(0)=\mathbf Q$, its highest line and positive-root kernel are its whole space, and extension to $K$ gives the one-dimensional simple trivial module $K$.

The delivery adds no new nodes and leaves the statement and stmt_deps unchanged. Steps 1-4 (complete reducibility over Q): perfectness follows from the coroots spanning h together with x=1/2[h_a,x]. The image algebra a=r(g) is semisimple (surjective-image node) and has a nondegenerate trace form (faithful-trace-form node). I checked the Casimir commutation (dual-basis signs) and Tr c=dim a. Because g is perfect it acts as zero on the 1-dimensional M/W, so c(M) is inside W. Then c restricted to W is nonzero and invertible on the simple W, which replaces Milne's algebraically-closed Schur step validly over Q. The perfect-Lie hyperplane criterion and the induction on dimension finish this part. Steps 5-7: the sl2-invariant-complement node applies with no nilpotence or diagonalizability assumed. The lowering-string leaf over Qbar gives an integer eigenvalue, and row reduction gives a rational primitive vector. The string-vanishing leaf closes the string, so H is diagonalizable with integer eigenvalues. root-base-rational-integral-spans gives integral weights in P. Steps 8-12: a maximal weight gives a dominant highest vector and a surjection from M(lambda) (I checked the generators of the left ideal). In the Verma module the finite-support Lagrange projectors show the sum of proper submodules is proper, so the simple quotient is unique. Both inequalities lambda<=mu<=lambda pin the singular line. Scalar endomorphisms follow from cyclicity. Absolute simplicity holds for arbitrary K because the rational matrix kernel commutes with extension.
